title: EvenUp's valuation soared past $1 billion on the potential of its AI. The startup has relied on humans to do much of the work, former employees say.
author: Ben Bergman

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of selective, human-led deployment and adds a concrete legal-service case study. EvenUp’s experience shows that task complexity changes the required human contribution, while consequential omissions can turn nominal review into substantial correction and completion work. Competing employee, company and customer accounts also reinforce the cluster’s caution that claimed efficiency and technical improvement do not by themselves establish reliable organisational value.
qs: "I thought that it was going to be like you check work that the AI has already done for you."  The reality, these people said, was that they had to work long hours to spot, correct, and complete tasks that the AI system could not handle with full accuracy.

"Some demands are generated and finalized using mostly AI, with a small amount of human input needed, while other more complicated demands require extensive human input but time is still saved by using the AI."  ### AI's virtuous cycle of improvement  It's a common strategy for AI companies to rely on humans early on to complete tasks and refine approaches.

kp.k: Rapid valuation growth rests on legal automation potential
kp.d: Business Insider reports that EvenUp rose from an $85 million valuation at the start of 2024 to more than $1 billion in an October funding round. Its proposed automation concerns personal-injury demands: extracting information from uploaded medical records and case files to help determine compensation. Investor enthusiasm is reported as a claim about potential, rather than demonstrated automation performance.
qs: EvenUp aims to streamline personal-injury demands and has said it is one of the fastest-growing companies in history after jumping from an $85 million valuation at the start of the year to unicorn status in an October funding round.
One of EvenUp's investors has described its "AI-based approach" as representing a "quantum leap forward."

kp.k: Former employees report substantial human production
kp.d: Eight former employees interviewed in late summer and early fall told Business Insider that humans performed a significant share of the work and AI was slow to assume it. Three described supervisors telling them at various points in 2024 not to use the AI; another said the instruction was close correction rather than nonuse. These are anonymous employee accounts, with anonymity requested to protect future job prospects.
qs: The reality, at least so far, is that human staff have done a significant share of that work, and EvenUp's AI has been slow to pick up the slack, eight former EvenUp employees told Business Insider in interviews over the late summer and early fall.
In practice, once you start with the company, my experience was that my managers told me not even to use the AI. They said it was unreliable and created too many errors.
I was 100% told it's not super reliable, and I need to have a really close eye on it

kp.k: EvenUp defends case-dependent human and AI collaboration
kp.d: CEO Rami Karabibar presents human involvement as a quality feature rather than a failure of automation. He distinguishes demands finalized mostly through AI with limited human input from complicated demands requiring extensive human input, while claiming time savings in both. The company's published explanation likewise says high-quality demand drafting requires more than automation.
qs: The combined approach ensures maximum accuracy and the highest quality

Some demands are generated and finalized using mostly AI, with a small amount of human input needed, while other more complicated demands require extensive human input but time is still saved by using the AI.
While AI models trained on generic data can handle some tasks, the complexity of drafting high-quality demand letters requires much more than automation alone

kp.k: Reported errors threaten compensation unless humans intervene
kp.d: Former employees described missed injuries, fabricated conditions and doctor visits, multiple hospital visits collapsed into one, incorrect injury locations and vehicle directions, and omitted medical findings connecting an injury to an accident. Three said uncaught mistakes could potentially reduce payouts. Business Insider found no instances reaching the final product; the spokesman acknowledged the reported problems could have occurred, especially in earlier AI versions, and cited human backstops.
qs: For instance, the software has missed key injuries in medical records while hallucinating conditions that did not exist, according to some of the former employees.
BI found no instances of these errors making it into the final product.
Such mistakes, if not caught by human staff, could have potentially reduced payouts, three of the employees said.

The software has also sometimes left out key details, such as whether a doctor determined a patient's injury was caused by a particular accident — crucial information for assigning damages, according to some of the employees.

kp.k: Medical record variability complicates reliable AI extraction
kp.d: University of Toronto law professor Abdi Aidid attributes some practical difficulty to differently formatted medical records and handwritten marginal notes. His explanation concerns input quality and interpretation, not a measured EvenUp error rate. The article places this within a broader concern about gaps between generative-AI ambitions and practical deployment.
qs: While AI is adept at sorting and interpreting vast amounts of data, it has so far struggled to accurately decipher content such as medical records that are formatted differently and often feature doctors' handwriting scribbled in the margins, said Abdi Aidid, an assistant professor of law at the University of Toronto who has built machine-learning tools.
When you scan the data, it gets scrambled a lot, and having AI read the scrambled data is not helpful

kp.k: Improvement claims conflict with former employees' experience
kp.d: The article explains the expected mechanism whereby human work supplies inputs that improve AI over time, but former employees saw little evidence of that cycle at EvenUp. Karabibar asserts continuous improvement. A spokesman reports 20% less employee time spent writing demands than at the beginning of 2024 and AI-originated drafts for 72% of content, versus 63% in June 2023, while declining to specify how much time AI itself saves.
qs: It didn't seem to me like the AI was improving
Our AI is improving every day
The startup's spokesman declined to specify how much time its AI saves but told BI that employees spend 20% less time writing demand letters than they did at the beginning of the year.
The spokesman also said 72% of demand letter content is started from an AI draft, up from 63% in June 2023.

kp.k: Customer values efficiency alongside human verification
kp.d: Robert Simon, cofounder of the Simon Law Group and a customer introduced to Business Insider by EvenUp, says the service increases his personal-injury firm's efficiency and human review reduces errors. His endorsement supports a combined service model, but is customer testimony rather than an independent accuracy measurement.
qs: Robert Simon, the cofounder of the Simon Law Group, said EvenUp's AI has made his personal-injury firm more efficient, and using humans reduces errors.
I appreciate that because I would love to have an extra set of eyes on it before the product comes back to me
EvenUp is highly, highly accurate.

kp.k: Investor sees human work creating proprietary training data
kp.d: Bain Capital Ventures partner Sarah Hinkfuss, an investor introduced by EvenUp, values employees' contribution to training models that competitors such as OpenAI cannot easily replicate. Her earlier blog post claims novel datasets and process automation significantly increase gross margins; the article supplies no margin figures.
qs: Sarah Hinkfuss, a partner at Bain Capital Ventures, said she appreciated EvenUp's human workers because they help train AI models that can't easily be replicated by competitors like OpenAI and its ChatGPT product.
They're building novel datasets that did not exist before, and they are automating processes that significantly boost gross margins

kp.k: Verification and completion work extend employee hours
kp.d: Most former employees said expectations of heavily automated work attracted them, but they instead spent long hours checking, correcting and completing outputs. Four reported simple cases could take as little as two hours, complex cases sometimes eight hours, and workdays could reach 16 hours. Accounts also describe work until 3 a.m., weekends and holidays; these are reported experiences rather than workforce-wide time measurements.
qs: You have to pretty much double-check everything the AI gives you or do it completely from scratch
A lot of my coworkers would work until 3 a.m. and on weekends to try to keep up with what was expected

EvenUp's AI could be helpful in simple cases that could be completed in as little as two hours. But more complex cases sometimes required eight hours, so a workday could stretch to 16 hours, four of the former employees said.
They [the managers] acted like it should be really quick because the AI did everything. But it didn't.

kp.k: Company disputes recruitment expectations and predicts easier work
kp.d: EvenUp's spokesman says candidates are warned that the role is challenging and writing-intensive, describes retention as comparable to other hyper-growth startups, and reports that 40% of legal operations associates were promoted in the third quarter of 2024. He predicts improving AI will make using the technology easier. The article also notes a vice president of people was hired at the end of October, emphasizing continuing human staffing needs.
qs: EvenUp's spokesman said candidates are told upfront the job is challenging and requires a substantial amount of writing.
He said retention rates are "in line with other hyper-growth startups" and that 40% of legal operations associates were promoted in the third quarter of this year.
In addition, as our AI continues to improve, leveraging our technology will become easier and easier.

kp.k: Founders frame automation as improving injury victims' compensation
kp.d: EvenUp's founders describe a mission to improve personal-injury victims' position, illustrated by an investor's account of cofounder Raymond Mieszaniec's father receiving an insufficient settlement after disabling injuries. In an interview the previous year, Mieszaniec claimed the technology automated medical-record interpretation and extraction while preserving quality and cost-effectiveness for firms. The article contrasts that promotional claim with former employees' accounts, rather than establishing improved victim outcomes.
qs: Karabibar, Raymond Mieszaniec, and Saam Mashhad started EvenUp to "even" the playing field for personal-injury victims.
We've trained a machine to be able to read through medical records, interpret the information it's scanning through, and extract the critical pieces of information

We are the first technology that has ever been created to essentially automate this entire process and also keep the quality high while ensuring these firms get all this work in a cost-effective manner.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source contrasts EvenUp's claims of automated, cost-effective personal-injury demand preparation with former employees' accounts of substantial manual work and verification.
pts.d: Cofounder Raymond Mieszaniec claimed in a prior interview that EvenUp could automate reading medical records, extracting critical information, and preparing work cost-effectively while maintaining quality. Ben Bergman reports that eight former employees instead described humans performing a significant share of the work, with limited perceived AI improvement. Three former employees said supervisors had at times instructed them not to use the AI; another reported instructions to scrutinize and correct it rather than avoid it. These are competing attributed accounts of the extent of automation, not an established finding that demand preparation is fully automated.

pts.k: EvenUp and a customer describe AI-assisted production with human review as improving efficiency while preserving accuracy; former employees describe verification and rewriting as substantial work.
pts.d: CEO Rami Karabibar says simpler demands can be produced mostly by AI, while complicated demands require extensive human input but still save time. EvenUp presents expert human review as a necessary feature rather than a temporary defect. Customer Robert Simon reports greater efficiency at his personal-injury firm and values the additional human review. Former employees describe checking nearly all output or starting again, with long hours needed to meet expectations that assumed greater automation. The operative model is therefore human-supervised assistance rather than unqualified autonomous delivery.

pts.k: Former employees claim AI extraction errors could reduce personal-injury recoveries if human reviewers failed to catch them.
pts.d: Reported errors include omitted injuries, fabricated medical conditions and doctor visits, aggregation of several hospital visits into one, incorrect injury locations or vehicle directions, and omission of doctors' causal links between accidents and injuries. Three former employees said uncaught errors could potentially reduce payouts. Bergman explicitly reports finding no instances of these errors reaching the final product. EvenUp's spokesman acknowledged that the problems could have occurred, particularly in earlier versions, and identified human review as the safeguard.

pts.k: EvenUp predicts continuing productivity improvement, while its investor argues that human-assisted production builds proprietary datasets and improves margins.
pts.d: Karabibar claims AI saves progressively more time, and the company's spokesman predicts its technology will become easier to use as it improves. Former employees dispute having observed meaningful improvement. Bain Capital Ventures partner Sarah Hinkfuss argues that human workers help create training datasets that competitors cannot easily replicate and that automation significantly boosts gross margins. Separately, Bergman frames EvenUp's rise from an $85 million valuation at the start of 2024 to more than $1 billion in October as investment driven by AI's automation potential, rather than as proof of realized automation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of employee interviews, company-reported production metrics, a selected customer's experience, investor assertions, and technical expert commentary—not independent performance benchmarking.
pts.d: Bergman interviewed eight anonymous former employees in late summer and early fall 2024; they requested anonymity to protect job prospects. Four described simple cases taking as little as two hours and complicated cases sometimes taking eight hours, with workdays potentially stretching to 16 hours. EvenUp reports 20% less employee time spent writing demand letters than at the start of the year and says 72% of demand-letter content starts from an AI draft, versus 63% in June 2023. These measure reported writing time and draft origin, respectively; neither establishes the amount of time saved specifically by AI or the share of final work completed autonomously. EvenUp declined to specify AI time savings. The company introduced BI to Simon and Hinkfuss, whose accounts provide customer experience and an investor's business rationale. University of Toronto law professor and machine-learning tool builder Abdi Aidid supplies an expert explanation of difficulties processing irregularly formatted and handwritten medical records. No independent accuracy test, quantified error rate, or margin analysis is supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The account concerns implementation through 2024; benefits depend on case complexity, input quality, model version, and human oversight, while future improvement has no specified completion date.
pts.d: Employee accounts were collected in late summer and early fall 2024 and include experiences earlier that year. Mieszaniec's broad automation claim comes from an interview described as occurring the previous year. The company's writing-time comparison runs from the beginning of 2024 to the reporting period, while the AI-draft comparison starts in June 2023. EvenUp qualifies the balance of human and AI work by demand complexity and suggests reported errors may relate especially to earlier AI versions. Aidid identifies inconsistent formatting and handwriting as constraints on medical-record processing. The potential reduction in payouts is conditional on errors escaping human review, not a reported realized outcome. Daily improvement and easier future use are company claims without a dated target for full automation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are personal-injury firms and their clients, EvenUp's production staff, and the company and its investors.
pts.d: Personal-injury firms are offered faster, cost-effective preparation of demand letters and more accurate extraction of facts relevant to compensation. Accident victims could benefit from better-supported demands, while uncaught omissions or inaccuracies could potentially lower recoveries; the article does not establish actual payout harm or improved settlement outcomes. EvenUp workers bear the manual drafting, correction, and verification burden, with former employees reporting late-night, weekend, and holiday work when productivity expectations exceeded automation capabilities. The title 'legal operations associate' here describes EvenUp's provider-side workforce, not corporate buyer-side legal operations. For EvenUp and its investors, the claimed commercial effects are valuation growth, better gross margins, and proprietary training data. The source does not demonstrate profession-wide displacement, staffing changes at law firms, or reduced unmet civil legal need.
